doc.title: Peter Vacher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

title: King Oliver, Armstrong and British trad enthusiasts
summary: Humphrey Lyttelton, Sandy Brown and Al Fairweather loved the Oliver and Hot Five records; Vacher and friends played new records down the phone.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Remembering King Oliver: the man, the band, the decline

blocks.x: Yes we do. I was going to run a few names by you and just maybe make a comment on them. Actually King Oliver was going to be a name.

Again you see at the time I came up or got interested, there was a terrific focus, I mean people like Humphrey Lyttelton were enamored of the work particularly of the King Oliver Creole Jazz Band. And then of course the Louis Armstrong Hot Five. Sandy

Brown and Al Fairweather were, you know, bowled over by that group of original innovators. Then a slightly later group became very involved with Bunk Johnson and George Lewis. So where I stood was on the King Oliver, Louis Armstrong, Kid Ory line. And I think I can remember buying my first 78 of the King Oliver Band, you know, “Canal Street Blues,” I mean we knew this was the real thing. And of course the young Louis was in there so that was powerful. To give you a little insight, not to ask, but I remember interviewing Al Fairweather who was Sandy Brown’s trumpet player, a wonderful trumpet player, very Louis Armstrong based. And he was describing the sort of formative experience that he and Sandy Brown went through. They were both at the same school. It’s a bit parallel to my story but they were much more talented. They would walk along Edinburgh, the High Street in Edinburgh, singing the respective clarinet and trumpet parts of each of the Hot Five tracks in a row. And they could do that. The music was sort of so powerful they’d absorbed it. See we all used to listen to records in a very intense sort of way. My friend was the trumpet player I mentioned to you. If I got a new record I’d ring him up you see, I’d phone him up. I’d play the record to him over the phone. I’m holding the phone over the old fashioned type phonograph as you would call it, and he’d say, “Put it on again.” And I’d play it again. And if he got a new record he’d do the same for me. It’s daft, isn’t it. That was the enthusiasm.
You have to be that way if you’re going to do something close to the music.
And the truth is we knew those early recordings far better than the ones we’ve got now. Because we played them over and over.
